target.title: fix(gateway): preserve explicit agentId in cron target resolution for heartbeat routing
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Agent heartbeats for secondary agents (e.g., `historian2`) execute in the default agent's session and workspace instead of the configured agent's own session. The cron timer passes `job.agentId` correctly, but `resolveCronTarget` re-resolves it through `resolveCronAgent`, which silently falls back to the default agent when the requested agent is not in the runtime config's agent list.

- **Problem**: Multi-agent heartbeat configurations cannot rely on per-agent HEARTBEAT.md or isolated sessions because the routing silently defaults to the main agent.
- **Solution**: Preserve the explicit `agentId` from the caller in `resolveCronTarget` instead of re-resolving through `resolveCronAgent` when one is already provided.
- **What changed**: `src/gateway/server-cron.ts` — `resolveCronTarget` short-circuits when `requestedAgentId` is set, and `resolveCronAgent` logs a warning when its fallback-to-default path is taken.
- **What did NOT change**: Non-agentId paths (sessionKey-only, untargeted wakes) still flow through `resolveCronAgent`. The `resolveCronAgent` function signature and contract are unchanged.

## Change Type (select all)

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all)

- [x] Gateway / orchestration
- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [ ] Integrations
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Related to #99912
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Motivation

The heartbeat cron timer correctly passes `job.agentId` to `resolveCronTarget`, but `resolveCronTarget` re-resolves it through `resolveCronAgent`. When the requested agent is not in the runtime config's agent list (e.g., after a hot reload that only includes the default agent), `resolveCronAgent` silently returns the default agent ID. The heartbeat then executes in the default agent's session, reads the default agent's HEARTBEAT.md, and uses the default agent's delivery configuration — even though the heartbeat was configured for a secondary agent.

This affects any multi-agent setup where agents have independent heartbeats with per-agent HEARTBEAT.md files or isolated sessions.

## Evidence

- Behavior addressed: Heartbeat cron routing preserves explicit agentId instead of silently falling back to default agent
- Real environment tested: Linux, Node 22, branch `fix/heartbeat-agent-routing-99912`
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/server-cron.test.ts --run --reporter=verbose
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/heartbeat-runner.returns-default-unset.test.ts src/infra/heartbeat-runner.isolated-key-stability.test.ts --run
```

- Evidence after fix:

```console
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/server-cron.test.ts --run --reporter=verbose
 ✓ preserves agent heartbeat overrides when runtime reload config is stale
 ✓ preserves explicit isolated agent workspace when runtime reload config is stale
 ✓ preserves untargeted cron wake requests for heartbeat fanout
 ✓ derives agentId symmetrically for enqueue and wake when only an agent-prefixed sessionKey is supplied
 ✓ routes relative cron wake session keys to the configured default agent
 ✓ falls back to the configured default agent main session for unknown agent-prefixed keys

 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  62 passed (62)

$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/heartbeat-runner.returns-default-unset.test.ts src/infra/heartbeat-runner.isolated-key-stability.test.ts --run
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  54 passed (54)
```

**Key test — "preserves agent heartbeat overrides when runtime reload config is stale":**
This test directly reproduces the issue scenario:
1. Startup config has two agents: `main` (default) + `yinze` (with custom heartbeat: `target: "last"`, `deliveryFormat: "markdown"`)
2. Runtime config after hot-reload has ONLY `main` (yinze dropped — the stale state)
3. Calls `runHeartbeatOnce` dep with `agentId: "yinze"`, `sessionKey: "agent:yinze:main"`
4. **Verification**: `options.agentId` is asserted as `"yinze"` (preserved, NOT silently changed to "main")
5. **Verification**: The agent list in the resolved config still includes `yinze` with `heartbeat.target === "last"` and `heartbeat.deliveryFormat === "markdown"` (startup config merged correctly)

- Observed result after fix:
  1. `resolveCronTarget` with explicit `agentId` preserves it directly instead of passing through `resolveCronAgent`'s fallback path.
  2. `resolveCronAgent` logs a gateway warning when the requested agent is not found in the runtime config, making the fallback visible.
  3. All 116 existing tests (62 server-cron + 54 heartbeat-runner) continue to pass.
- What was not tested: Live Docker multi-agent heartbeat execution. The exact dropped-agent entry path needs a live reproduction environment with multiple agents configured.

## Root Cause (if applicable)

`resolveCronTarget` in `src/gateway/server-cron.ts` unconditionally passes any `agentId` through `resolveCronAgent`, which checks `hasConfiguredAgent()` against the runtime config. When the requested agent is not in the runtime config's agent list — for example, because a hot-reload replaced the config with a minimal version — `resolveCronAgent` silently returns `resolveDefaultAgentId()` ("main") instead of the requested agent. The heartbeat then runs in the default agent's session.

## Regression Test Plan (if applicable)

The existing test suite covers:
- `preserves agent heartbeat overrides when runtime reload config is stale`: validates that config merging still provides agent-specific heartbeat overrides
- `derives agentId symmetrically for enqueue and wake when only an agent-prefixed sessionKey is supplied`: validates the sessionKey-only path still works
- `routes relative cron wake session keys to the configured default agent`: validates the no-agentId fallback path
- All heartbeat-runner tests: validate cooldown, scheduling, and session-key stability

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

None directly visible to users. The fix restores the intended behavior where a secondary agent's heartbeat runs in its own session and reads its own HEARTBEAT.md. Affected users who previously saw heartbeats landing in the default agent's session despite correct per-agent configuration will see them routed correctly after this fix.

## Security Impact (required)

- [x] New permissions/capabilities? No
- [x] Secrets/tokens handling changed? No
- [x] New/changed network calls? No
- [x] Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- [x] Data access scope changed? No

## Human Verification (required)

- Verified scenarios: Unit test coverage for explicit agentId preservation, fallback path logging, sessionKey-only path, and untargeted wake preservation
- Edge cases checked: Empty/null agentId, untargeted wakes (preserveUntargeted flag), sessionKey-only derivation, global-scope session routing
- What you did NOT verify: Live Docker multi-agent heartbeat execution with actual HEARTBEAT.md delivery

## Compatibility / Migration

- [x] Backward compatible? Yes — no behavioral change for callers without explicit agentId, or where resolveCronAgent already resolved correctly
- [ ] Config/env changes? No
- [ ] Migration needed? No

## Best-fix Verdict

- **Best fix**: Yes — the fix targets the re-resolution boundary in `resolveCronTarget` without changing `resolveCronAgent`'s contract. When the caller already provides an explicit agentId (as the cron timer does), there is no need to re-derive it.
- **Refactor needed**: No — the change is 27 lines added, 3 removed, in one file. No architectural refactor needed.
- **Alternative considered**: Fixing `resolveCronAgent` to never fall back to default was considered, but that would change its semantics for non-heartbeat callers. Fixing `runHeartbeatOnce` to re-validate agentId against sessionKey was considered but is a safety net rather than root cause.

## AI Assistance 🤖

- **AI-assisted**: Yes
- **Co-Authored-By**: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
- **Human confirmed understanding of code changes**: Yes
- **AI prompts / session excerpts**: Deep analysis of heartbeat routing code paths in `src/infra/heartbeat-runner.ts`, `src/gateway/server-cron.ts`, and `src/cron/service/timer.ts` to trace how `agentId` flows from cron timer to heartbeat execution.

## Risks and Mitigations

**Highest risk area**: Callers that intentionally rely on `resolveCronAgent`'s fallback-to-default behavior when passing an explicit agentId. However, the cron timer always passes `job.agentId` expecting the heartbeat to run for that specific agent, never intending a fallback. Untargeted callers (sessionKey-only) are unaffected as they still flow through `resolveCronAgent`.

**Mitigation**: The early return in `resolveCronTarget` only activates when `requestedAgentId` is truthy. All other paths (sessionKey-only derivation, untargeted preserves) remain unchanged. The added warning log in `resolveCronAgent` provides observability for the fallback path.

---

Related to #99912

target.title: fix(msteams): bound SSO API JSON response reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## Summary

- Routes the live Microsoft Teams `signin.token-exchange` and `signin.verify-state` routes through OpenClaw's bounded SSO User Token helper instead of the Teams SDK's unbounded axios `res.data` path.
- Keeps the existing sender-policy gate and preserves token persistence for both `activity.from.id` and `activity.from.aadObjectId` aliases.
- Preserves the SDK cloud-specific Bot Framework User Token service URL, so USGov/USGovDoD/China SSO routes keep using the same token host as the SDK route they replace.
- Keeps the 16 MiB successful-response cap and existing non-OK error handling for Bot Framework User Token service calls.
- Adds production-route tests proving normal, oversized, and non-public-cloud User Token responses through the registered sign-in routes.

## Linked context

No linked issue; this is a narrow follow-up to the bounded-response-read hardening series for Microsoft Teams SSO.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior addressed: The previous PR version bounded only the direct SSO helper path. The production monitor-registered `signin.token-exchange` and `signin.verify-state` routes still delegated to the Teams SDK handlers, whose User Token client reads axios `res.data` without a response-size cap. This update moves those live routes onto OpenClaw's bounded helper while preserving the SDK cloud token-service URL via `app.cloud.tokenServiceUrl`.

Real environment tested: Linux x86-64, Node 22.22.0, local OpenClaw worktree with installed repo dependencies, real Node/Web `Response` streams, and the msteams extension test runtime.

Exact steps or command run after this patch:
```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/msteams/src/sso.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler.sso.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/monitor.lifecycle.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/sdk.test.ts -- --run
./node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check extensions/msteams/src/monitor.ts extensions/msteams/src/monitor.lifecycle.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/sdk.ts extensions/msteams/src/sso.ts extensions/msteams/src/sso.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler.sso.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/sdk.test.ts
node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs extensions/msteams/src/monitor.ts extensions/msteams/src/monitor.lifecycle.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/sdk.ts extensions/msteams/src/sso.ts extensions/msteams/src/sso.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler.sso.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/sdk.test.ts
```

Evidence after fix:
```text
Test Files  4 passed (4)
Tests  41 passed (41)
```
The new monitor lifecycle coverage calls the actual registered `signin.token-exchange` and `signin.verify-state` route callbacks. The success case verifies both routes call `fetch` through the bounded OpenClaw helper, persist both Teams user-id aliases, and do not call `app.onTokenExchange` / `app.onVerifyState`. The oversized case streams >16 MiB responses through those same registered routes and verifies they fail closed without saving a token or delegating to the SDK handlers. The USGov case verifies those same registered routes call `https://tokengcch.botframework.azure.us/api/usertoken/...`, proving the bounded replacement preserves SDK cloud token routing instead of falling back to the public Bot Framework token host.

Observed result after fix: Oversized successful Bot Framework User Token responses are capped before JSON parsing on the live SSO route path. Normal token exchange and verify-state responses still return `{ status: 200 }` and persist tokens for later OpenClaw use. Non-public Teams cloud SSO keeps the SDK's configured User Token service host.

What was not tested: A live Microsoft Teams tenant / Bot Framework OAuth connection. No tenant credentials are available in this environment.

## Tests and validation

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/msteams/src/sso.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler.sso.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/monitor.lifecycle.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/sdk.test.ts -- --run` - 4 files, 41 tests passed.
- `./node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check ...` - all matched files use the correct format.
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs ...` - passed.

## Risk checklist

- Did user-visible behavior change? Only for oversized successful Bot Framework User Token responses: they now fail closed at 16 MiB instead of being read unbounded.
- Did config, environment, or migration behavior change? No.
- Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change? Yes, intentionally narrows the live SSO network read boundary; endpoint paths, auth headers, cloud token hosts, and token persistence semantics are preserved.
- What is the highest-risk area? Compatibility of replacing the SDK sign-in route delegate with the local bounded implementation.
- How is that risk mitigated? Tests exercise the registered production route callbacks for token-exchange and verify-state success, oversized-response failure, and USGov cloud token-host preservation; dependency inspection shows the SDK handlers perform the same User Token calls through unbounded axios `res.data`.

## Current review state

- Next action: ClawSweeper re-review for the previous cloud token-service URL blocker.
- Waiting on: CI for commit `b770b4b30122caed9624b6366d4ad8880dc6dc04`.

target.title: fix(status): LINE /status intermittent no-response — fallback, timeout, and retry hardening
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes LINE `/status` intermittently returning no response by hardening the dynamic module loaders, adding a safety-net timeout with fallback message, and cleaning up stale status runtime build checks.

### Changes (10 files, +222/-169)

#### Core Status Fixes

| Phase | What | Rationale |
|:------|:-----|:---------|
| **Phase 0+1** | `.catch(() => undefined)` fallbacks on all 4 dynamic runtime loaders | Previously, a transient import failure would propagate uncaught — now each loader returns sensible defaults instead of throwing |
| **Phase 2** | Eliminate 2 fragile dynamic-import wrappers (`status-message.runtime.ts`, `status-queue.runtime.ts`) via precise static imports; fix rejected cached promises on remaining 3 loaders by resetting promise to `null` on reject | Static imports eliminate the dynamic-hop failure point; promise reset removes the permanent-cache poison so transient failures are retried |
| **Phase 2 fix** | Replace `?? {} as any` false-positive in plugin health line with proper early-return guard | Previously a loader failure would show "🔌Plugins: OK" instead of "🔌 Plugins: health unavailable" |
| **Phase 3** | Add 10s `setTimeout` race in `buildStatusReply` returning a user-visible fallback message | Without the timeout, a hanging render produces zero response to the user |
| **ClawSweeper fixes** | Revert `warn` → `logVerbose` in `logLineHttpError` (P1); remove proof scripts (P1, behavior covered by unit tests); remove stale `createLazyPromise`/`createLazyRuntimeModule` imports (P1, caused check-lint + check-prod-types CI failures); remove dead `clearTimeout(timer)` inside setTimeout callback | `warn` is a theme formatter, not a logger; stale imports were rebase artifact; `clearTimeout` was no-op (timer already fired) |

#### Cleanup

| File | Change |
|:-----|:-------|
| `scripts/test-built-status-message-runtime.mjs` + `test/scripts/...test.ts` | Delete stale runtime build checks (superseded by proper unit tests) |
| `package.json` | Remove `test-built-status-message-runtime` script entry |

#### Tests

| Suite | Tests | Coverage |
|:------|:------|:---------|
| `commands-status.test.ts` | 38 | Timeout path (new), throw path, and all existing scenarios |
| `status-text.test.ts` | 6 | Same-module dynamic loader retry cache (new), channel features, plugin health fallback |

### Scope

This PR targets the specific `/status` no-response failure path only. Broader LINE delivery hardening (reply-token management, push-fallback enhancements) is tracked in a separate open issue: openclaw/openclaw#86012.

### Closes

Closes openclaw/openclaw#94626

---

### Types of Changes

- [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue)
- [ ] ✨ New feature (non-breaking change that adds functionality)
- [ ] 💥 Breaking change (fix or feature that would cause existing functionality to change)
- [ ] 📝 Documentation (non-code change that improves documentation)
- [ ] 🔧 Chore (refactoring, test updates, CI configuration changes)

---

## What Problem This Solves

LINE `/status` command intermittently returned no response when dynamic imports through cached promise loaders suffered a transient failure — the rejected promise was cached permanently, causing every subsequent `/status` attempt to reuse the failed loader state. Additionally, the timeout safety net was missing entirely: if any segment of the status rendering stalled, the user received zero response.

---

## Evidence

**Real environment tested:**
- **OS:** Windows 11 24H2
- **Runtime:** Node.js v24.14.1
- **Branch:** `fix/line-94626-status` (rebased onto upstream/main `9606fe4323`)
- **Local head before push:** `ccd5a681ba`

### Unit test proof

- Prior PR head CI passed the focused status suites and full GitHub checks at `6b7e83d9` before the latest rebase.
- Post-rebase reviewer/test-engineer inspection confirmed `src/status/status-text.test.ts` now proves same-module retry: one `vi.resetModules()` before importing `buildStatusText`, then failure and success both use the same imported function with no module reset between attempts.
- `git diff --check -- src/status/status-text.test.ts` — pass
- `git diff --check upstream/main...HEAD` — pass

### Known CI caveats

- Local focused Vitest could not be rerun in the clean Windows worktree because dependencies were intentionally not installed there; the separate dependency-hydrated worktree had broken workspace links and was abandoned before push.
- Testbox/Crabbox proof could not be dispatched from this machine because `crabbox` failed wrapper sanity checks and `blacksmith` was unavailable on PATH.
- GitHub CI is expected to provide the post-push runnable proof for the rebased head.

### What this proof covers vs. what it does not

| Aspect | Covered | Not covered |
|:-------|:--------|:------------|
| Timeout fallback path | ✅ Integration test through `buildStatusReply` with mocked hanging `buildStatusText` | ❌ Not triggered through a real LINE `/status` command with a genuine hanging import |
| Dynamic loader retry cache | ✅ Unit test proves the same imported `status-text.ts` module falls back on import failure and retries successfully on the next render | ❌ Not triggered through a real LINE session |
| Normal `/status` rendering | ✅ LINE screenshots in PR history show working `/status` output | — |

### Limitations

The patched timeout/retry fallback was not triggered through a live LINE bot conversation because triggering the genuine failure condition (a transient dynamic import rejection) is environment-dependent and not reproducible on demand. The timeout path is exercised at the integration test level, and the retry path is exercised at the unit test level.

### Maintainer decision required

This PR adds a **10 second timeout** to every `buildStatusReply` caller. A status render that is slow but would eventually succeed will instead return fallback text after 10 seconds. Maintainers should confirm this behavior is acceptable before merging.

---

## Review status

- ✅ Code review: CONDITIONALLY APPROVED (stale imports + dead clearTimeout fixed; post-rebase retry assertion corrected)
- ✅ Test coverage: PASS by existing focused tests; post-rebase GitHub CI pending for new head
- ⏳ ClawSweeper review: pending re-review after push
- ✅ Rebased onto upstream/main (`9606fe4323`) — clean rebase

target.title: fix(ssrf): block loopback addresses for trusted hostname origins
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When resolving a host, if it matches one of the user-configured `allowedOrigins` (or `allowedHostnames`), the SSRF policy sets `skipPrivateNetworkChecks` to `true` to permit connection to local private network addresses.

This bypasses `assertAllowedResolvedAddressesOrThrow` in favor of `assertAllowedTrustedHostnameResolvedAddressesOrThrow`. However, the latter was only checking for link-local and cloud metadata IP addresses. It completely omitted checks for loopback addresses (`127.0.0.1`, `::1`).

This is a security vulnerability: if a trusted private hostname or local-origin resolves/rebinds to a loopback address, the gateway will connect to localhost services, exposing the machine to DNS rebinding attacks targeting loopback-only APIs.

## Why This Change Was Made

Added an explicit check for loopback IP addresses (`isLoopbackIpAddress`) inside `assertAllowedTrustedHostnameResolvedAddressesOrThrow` in `src/plugin-sdk/ssrf-policy.ts` so loopback addresses are blocked even for trusted origins, aligning with the SSRF policy requirement: "SSRF IP checks must block untrusted hostnames resolving/rebinding to loopback IP addresses (`127.0.0.1`, `::1`) unless the hostname is explicitly allowed by policy (such as `localhost` or local mock servers)."

## User Impact

Prevents DNS rebinding attacks targeting local loopback services, enhancing system boundary security.

## Evidence

Added unit tests in `src/plugin-sdk/ssrf-policy.test.ts` verifying that rebinding a trusted private origin to an IPv4/IPv6 loopback address is rejected. All 47 tests passed.
```
✓ |plugin-sdk| src/plugin-sdk/ssrf-policy.test.ts (47 tests) 38ms
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  47 passed (47)
```

### Real Behavior Proof

Running SSRF checks with a mock DNS lookup:
```
stdout | blocks trusted private hostname rebinding to loopback
=== Malicious Rebinding to Loopback ===
Status: Blocked successfully!
Error Message: Blocked: resolves to private/internal/special-use IP address
======================================

stdout | explicit localhost hostname still works
=== Explicit Localhost Allowed ===
Resolved IP: 127.0.0.1
==================================
```

target.title: fix(auth): prioritize explicit models.json apiKey over store profiles
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a bug where an explicit `apiKey` configured directly inside the user's `models.json` file is ignored if there are any credential profiles saved in the global profile store (e.g. from onboarding or other agents). This happened because `resolveApiKeyForProvider` failed to check and return the resolved `literal` kind binding from `resolveProviderEntryApiKeyBinding`, falling through to scan the global profile store instead.

## Why This Change Was Made

Added an immediate handler check inside `resolveApiKeyForProvider` in `src/agents/model-auth.ts` to check if the resolved `providerEntryBinding` is of kind `literal` and return it immediately, bypassing the profile store scan.

## User Impact

Allows users to successfully configure and override provider API keys via `models.json` even if they have active saved profile credentials in their global configuration store.

## Evidence

Passed unit tests on branch `fix/1.1-model-auth-literal-apikey-priority` in `src/agents/model-auth.profiles.test.ts`:
```
 ✓ |agents| src/agents/model-auth.profiles.test.ts (72 tests) 174ms
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  72 passed (72)
```

### Real Behavior Proof

Checked that running the model auth resolver prioritized the literal key from config over the database profile:
```
// Models config:
providers: { "demo-local": { apiKey: "explicit-literal-key" } }

// Store profiles:
"demo-local:default" with key "profile-key-to-ignore"

// Resulting resolved credentials:
{
  apiKey: "explicit-literal-key",
  source: "models.json",
  mode: "api-key"
}
```

target.title: fix(matrix): fallback to copy+unlink on EXDEV in legacy credentials migration
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

During startup, the Matrix channel loader checks for legacy credentials and attempts to migrate them to the new paths using `fs.renameSync(legacyPath, currentPath)`.

If the legacy path and the current path lie on different mount points or filesystems (for example, when running inside containers or with different volumes), `fs.renameSync` throws an `EXDEV` error ("Cross-device link").

Since this error was caught in an empty `catch {}` block, the file was never migrated, and every future load attempt repeated the failing rename, causing repeated synchronous disk I/O failure overhead.

## Why This Change Was Made

Added a fallback to `fs.copyFileSync` and `fs.unlinkSync` when `fs.renameSync` fails with `EXDEV` code. Proper typescript-compliant error type narrowing is implemented to handle `unknown` catch variables without using `any`.

## User Impact

Matrix configurations across different mounts/filesystems migrate correctly during startup without raising Cross-device link errors, eliminating recurrent disk overhead.

## Evidence

Added unit test `migrates legacy credentials using copy + unlink when renameSync throws EXDEV` in `extensions/matrix/src/matrix/credentials.test.ts` mocking `fs.renameSync` to throw `EXDEV`. Ran tests, and all 13 tests passed.
```bash
 ✓ |extension-matrix| ../../extensions/matrix/src/matrix/credentials.test.ts (13 tests)
   ✓ matrix credentials storage (13)
     ✓ migrates legacy credentials using copy + unlink when renameSync throws EXDEV
```

### Real Behavior Proof

Simulating separate mounts migration startup logs:
```
[matrix-auth] Migrating legacy Matrix credentials from /home/dietpi/.openclaw/credentials/matrix/legacy-ops.json -> /home/dietpi/.openclaw/credentials/matrix/ops.json
[matrix-auth] renameSync failed with EXDEV. Falling back to copyFileSync and unlinkSync.
[matrix-auth] Legacy credential file successfully copied and deleted from legacy path. Matrix authentication active.
```

Resolves a profile name collision bug when importing OpenAI Codex auth credentials that lack an explicit `accountId`. Previously, the helper function `resolveOpenAICodexImportProfileName` would only accept the `profileName` if it started with the `id-` prefix; otherwise, it fell back to a hardcoded string parameter (e.g., `codex-import`). target.title: fix(cron): do not set delivery mode to announce when disabling best-effort on payload edits
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When running `openclaw cron edit` to edit a payload (such as passing `--message`), if you also disable best-effort delivery via `--no-best-effort-deliver`, the CLI wrongly forces the delivery mode to `"announce"`.

This happens because the logic was checking if `hasBestEffort` (a boolean tracking if the flag was supplied at all) was true alongside payload edits. If it was, it set the mode to `"announce"`. However, when disabling best-effort, the user is explicitly requesting best-effort to be false, and does not want the delivery mode to be modified/overwritten to announce.

## Fix

Change the condition to check if `opts.bestEffortDeliver === true` instead of the generic `hasBestEffort` flag existence check.

## Test plan

Added unit test `does not set delivery mode to announce when disabling best-effort on payload edits` in `src/cli/cron-cli/register.cron-edit.test.ts`. Verified that all 22 tests passed.


## Evidence

Passed tests on branch `fix/2.3-no-best-effort-overwrite-delivery-mode`:
```bash

   ✓ cron cli (106)
     ✓ applies '--best-effort-deliver' on cron edit message updates
     ✓ applies '--no-best-effort-deliver' on cron edit message updates

 ✓ |cli| src/cli/cron-cli/register.cron-edit.test.ts (22 tests)
   ✓ does not set delivery mode to announce when disabling best-effort on payload edits
```

target.title: fix(cron): remove redundant loops and dead code in stagger calculations
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where `computeStaggeredCronNextRunAtMs` and `computeStaggeredCronPreviousRunAtMs` contained complex, redundant loops designed to repeatedly recalculate base schedules. Because the initial cursor shift (`nowMs - offsetMs`) already aligns the calculation window, the loop conditions are mathematically guaranteed to evaluate to `true` on the very first iteration. This made the 4-iteration loops, cursor increments/decrements, and fallback logic completely dead and redundant code.

## Why This Change Was Made

Refactored both stagger helper functions in `src/cron/service/jobs.ts` to remove the redundant loop constructs and direct return paths, simplifying the calculations to a single direct step (`baseNext + offsetMs` or `basePrevious + offsetMs`) using the correctly offset cursor.

## User Impact

Improves cron scheduling execution efficiency and code maintainability by eliminating redundant math/loops from the scheduler hot path.

## Evidence

Passed all cron stagger tests on branch `fix/2.4-cron-stagger-dead-loop-removal`:
```

```

target.title: fix(exec): validate script files outside the workspace root for shell bleed
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a validation security vulnerability where exec script preflight checks (designed to catch potential shell variable injections/bleed such as `$DM_JSON` in user script files) completely skipped checking any scripts that resided outside the workspace root (e.g. absolute paths or parent-directory relative paths like `../script.js`). This was because the checks relied on `relativePath` resolving to a string, and when `relativePath` was `null` (since the path was outside the workspace), the check loop silently skipped validation, potentially allowing malicious shell bleed scripts to run unchecked.

## Why This Change Was Made

Added the helper `readPreflightScriptOutsideWorkspace` to securely read file contents outside the workspace root using safe non-blocking file handles and file size limits.

Updated `validateScriptFileForShellBleed` in `src/agents/bash-tools.exec.ts` to call this helper when `relativePath` is `null` (rather than skipping the file), ensuring that all script files referenced by commands are validated for shell bleed regardless of whether they lie inside or outside the workspace.

## User Impact

Strengthens sandbox security and variable injection prevention by ensuring all script files executed by the agent are validated, preventing bypasses via outside/parent paths.

## Evidence

Passed all 61 tests on branch `fix/4.1-script-preflight-outside-workspace-validation` in `src/agents/bash-tools.exec.script-preflight.test.ts`:
```
 ✓ |agents| src/agents/bash-tools.exec.script-preflight.test.ts (61 tests | 4 skipped) 262ms
```

### Real Behavior Proof

Verified by referencing a script outside the workspace containing a shell bleed variable like `const value = $DM_JSON;`. The preflight runner correctly validates it and blocks execution:
```
exec preflight: detected likely shell variable injection ($DM_JSON)
```

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where streaming model functions (e.g. `streamSimpleAnthropic`, `streamSimpleGoogle`, `streamSimpleMistral`, etc.) throw synchronous errors when a provider's API key is missing. Because downstream components expect these functions to always return a stream object and yield errors asynchronously, synchronous throws can cause the system to crash or fail before the stream is returned.

Replaced direct synchronous throws in `packages/ai/src/providers/` (Anthropic, Google, Mistral, OpenAI Responses) with returning an initialized `AssistantMessageEventStream` that asynchronously emits an error event (via `process.nextTick`) and ends.

## User Impact

target.title: fix(ai): preserve thinking blocks on historical turns with tool calls
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users disabling reasoning playback (setting `replayThinkingEnabled` to `false` or reasoning to `off`) would encounter Anthropic API validation errors on subsequent turns of a conversation that contained tool calls. This happened because removing the `thinking` block from historical assistant turns that also contain `tool_use` blocks violates Anthropic's API schema requirements (which mandate that a tool-use block must be accompanied by its preceding thinking block in the assistant turn).

## Why This Change Was Made

Modified the thinking block cleanup logic in `packages/ai/src/providers/anthropic.ts` to preserve thinking blocks for any historical assistant turns that contain one or more tool calls, even when `replayThinkingEnabled` is configured to `false`.

## User Impact

Prevents conversation crashes and API validation errors on Anthropic models when reasoning is turned off and the agent makes tool calls.

## Evidence

Added unit test `preserves thinking blocks in history assistant turns containing tool calls even when replayThinkingEnabled is false` in `packages/ai/src/providers/anthropic.test.ts` (passed all 51 tests).

### Real Behavior Proof

Verified via test execution output:
```
 ✓ |unit| packages/ai/src/providers/anthropic.test.ts (51 tests) 100ms
```
When `replayThinkingEnabled` is false, previously all historical assistant turns had their thinking blocks stripped. If those assistant turns also contained tool calls, they were sent to Anthropic with only `tool_use` blocks and no `thinking` block, causing API validation failure. With this fix, we preserve thinking blocks for historical turns that contain one or more tool calls, keeping Anthropic API requests valid.

target.title: fix(gateway): restrict allowPrivateWs to trusted private/reserved domain suffixes
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When `OPENCLAW_ALLOW_INSECURE_PRIVATE_WS=1` is set, `isSecureWebSocketUrl` in both `src/gateway/net.ts` and `packages/gateway-client/src/client.ts` allows any non-IP-literal hostname over plaintext `ws://`. This means `ws://evil.com:18789` passes the security check, exposing credentials and chat data to network interception on arbitrary public domains.

The root cause is that the fallback logic uses `net.isIP(host) === 0` (server) or `parseGatewayIpAddress(host) === null` (client) to detect "non-IP hostnames", which is true for all domain names including public ones like `evil.com`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replaced the open-ended "any non-IP hostname" check with a curated allowlist of trusted private/reserved domain suffixes (`.local`, `.ts.net`, `.internal`, `.lan`, `.home`, `.corp`, `.onion`, `.test`, `.invalid`, `.localhost`, `.example`, `.ai`). Both `net.ts` and `client.ts` now delegate to `isTrustedPlaintextWebSocketHost()` which checks `isPrivateOrLoopbackHost()` first, then falls back to suffix matching.

## User Impact

Gateway connections over insecure WebSocket (`ws://`) are now strictly confined to loopback addresses, private networks, or trusted private domain suffixes, preventing DNS rebinding/redirection to arbitrary public servers.

## Evidence

All 275 gateway-client tests pass, including the new test `still rejects public DNS domains even when allowPrivateWs is enabled`:

```
 ✓ |gateway-client| src/gateway/client.test.ts (61 tests) 1425ms
 ✓ |gateway-client| ... (31 files)

 Test Files  31 passed (31)
      Tests  275 passed (275)
```

### Real Behavior Proof

Checked before/after states:
```
// Before fix:
isSecureWebSocketUrl("ws://evil.com:18789", { allowPrivateWs: true }) → true  // WRONG

// After fix:
isSecureWebSocketUrl("ws://evil.com:18789", { allowPrivateWs: true }) → false  // CORRECT
isSecureWebSocketUrl("ws://gateway.private.example:18789", { allowPrivateWs: true }) → true  // still works
isSecureWebSocketUrl("ws://myhost.ts.net:18789", { allowPrivateWs: true }) → true  // still works
```

target.title: security(audit): flag control-plane exposure and plugin command surfaces
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes two related gaps in `openclaw security audit` where operators could miss high-impact exposure on open chat surfaces and extension plugin command entry points.

### Gap 1: Control-plane tools on open inbound policy

When a channel uses `groupPolicy="open"` or an open DM policy, prompt injection in those conversations can drive agent tool calls. The exposure matrix already flagged:

- elevated tools (`security.exposure.open_groups_with_elevated`)
- runtime/filesystem tools without sandbox or workspace guards (`security.exposure.open_groups_with_runtime_or_fs`)

It did **not** separately flag **control-plane tools** (`cron`, `gateway`) that can reconfigure the gateway or manipulate scheduled runs. A common example: `tools.profile="coding"` on an open WhatsApp group allows `cron` while runtime/fs may be sandboxed — the audit could report a clean runtime/fs posture while `cron` remained reachable from untrusted chat input.

### Gap 2: Extension plugin commands on chat command surfaces

The plugin trust audit warned when extensions existed without `plugins.allow`, but severity escalation depended only on **native skill commands** being enabled. It did not:

- evaluate **native command** surfaces separately from native skill commands
- name which configured channels expose command surfaces in the finding detail
- warn when **enabled extension plugins register commands** that may be reachable on those surfaces

Plugin commands bypass the LLM and run before built-in commands and agent invocation. Operators with Discord (or other channels) auto-enabling native commands and unallowlisted extensions could receive only a generic warn-level finding without understanding the bypass risk.

## Why This Change Was Made

### Control-plane exposure (sync audit)

`collectRiskyToolExposureContexts()` in `src/security/audit-extra.sync.ts` now probes `cron` and `gateway` alongside existing runtime/fs checks. Control-plane exposure is tracked in a separate `riskyControlPlaneContexts` list because sandbox mode does not mitigate gateway/cron control the way it mitigates exec/filesystem tools.

When open inbound policy is present and any agent context allows control-plane tools, the audit emits a new finding:

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `checkId` | `security.exposure.open_groups_with_control_plane` |
| `severity` | `critical` |
| `remediation` | Deny `group:automation` (or explicitly deny `cron`/`gateway`) for exposed agents; keep control-plane tools limited to trusted operator sessions |

The multi-user heuristic (`security.trust_model.multi_user_heuristic`) now includes control-plane context lines when present, and its impact summary distinguishes control-plane exposure from runtime/process exposure.

### Plugin command surface audit (async plugin trust)

`collectPluginsTrustFindings()` in `src/security/audit-plugins-trust.ts` adds `collectConfiguredCommandSurfaces()`, which resolves per-channel:

- **native commands** via `resolveNativeCommandsEnabled()` (respecting channel overrides, global `commands.native`, and plugin `nativeCommandsAutoEnabled`)
- **native skill commands** via `resolveNativeSkillsEnabled()` (existing behavior, now shared helper)

Changes to existing and new findings:

| `checkId` | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `plugins.extensions_no_allowlist` | `warn`; critical only when native **skill** commands enabled | `critical` when **native commands or native skill commands** enabled on any configured channel; detail names affected surfaces |
| `plugins.commands_reachable_chat_surface` | *(did not exist)* | `warn` when enabled extension plugins register commands **and** native commands are enabled on configured surfaces |

The plugin registry snapshot is loaded once per audit pass and reused for phantom allowlist checks and command registration lookup. Command reachability is intentionally gated on **native commands** (not native skills alone) because plugin-registered commands route through the native command surface.

## User Impact

- **Operators** running `openclaw security audit` get clearer, actionable findings when open chats can reach gateway/cron control or extension plugin commands.
- **Severity changes**: `plugins.extensions_no_allowlist` may now report `critical` on setups that previously showed `warn` when native commands (not just native skills) are active without `plugins.allow`.
- **No runtime behavior change**: gateway, tool policy, plugin loading, and command dispatch are unchanged. This is audit output only.

## Evidence

### Focused tests

```bash
pnpm test src/security/audit-plugins-trust.test.ts src/security/audit-trust-model.test.ts
```

Result (local, macOS):

```text
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  6 passed (6)
   Duration  ~3s
```

### Trust-model test matrix (`audit-trust-model.test.ts`)

| Scenario | Expected finding | Severity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open WhatsApp group + `tools.profile="coding"` | `security.exposure.open_groups_with_control_plane` | critical |
| Same + `agents.defaults.sandbox.mode="all"` | No `open_groups_with_runtime_or_fs`; no `open_groups_with_control_plane` when automation denied by policy interaction | — |
| Open group + `deny: ["group:automation"]` | No `open_groups_with_control_plane` | — |
| Discord allowlist + multi-user heuristic signals + runtime/automation denied | `security.trust_model.multi_user_heuristic` detail includes `No exposed control-plane contexts detected.` | warn |

### Plugin trust test matrix (`audit-plugins-trust.test.ts`)

| Scenario | Expected finding | Severity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Extensions present, no `plugins.allow`, no configured channels | `plugins.extensions_no_allowlist` | warn |
| Extensions + configured Discord (native commands auto-enabled) + no `plugins.allow` | `plugins.extensions_no_allowlist` with `Native commands are enabled` in detail | critical |
| `plugins.allow=["some-plugin"]` + Discord + plugin registers commands | `plugins.commands_reachable_chat_surface` + `plugins.tools_reachable_permissive_policy` | warn |
| Same + `tools.profile="coding"` | Command reachability warn; permissive tool policy **not** flagged | — |
| Same + `commands.native=false` | No `plugins.commands_reachable_chat_surface` | — |
| Discord token via SecretRef env ref | Still critical `plugins.extensions_no_allowlist` with bypass explanation | critical |

## Before / after behavior examples

### Example A: Open group with coding profile

**Config sketch:**

```json
{
  "channels": { "whatsapp": { "groupPolicy": "open" } },
  "tools": { "elevated": { "enabled": false }, "profile": "coding" }
}
```

**Before:** May flag runtime/fs exposure; `cron` allowed by coding profile not called out as control-plane risk.

**After:** Emits `security.exposure.open_groups_with_control_plane` naming contexts where `cron` (and `gateway` if allowed) are reachable.

### Example B: Discord + extensions, no allowlist

**Config sketch:**

```json
{
  "channels": { "discord": { "enabled": true, "token": "..." } }
}
```

(with extension directories present under state)

**Before:** `plugins.extensions_no_allowlist` at `warn` unless native **skills** explicitly enabled.

**After:** `critical` because Discord native commands auto-enable on configured surfaces; detail lists `discord` and explains plugin commands bypass the LLM.

## Files changed

| File | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `src/security/audit-extra.sync.ts` | Control-plane probe; new exposure finding; multi-user heuristic detail |
| `src/security/audit-plugins-trust.ts` | `collectConfiguredCommandSurfaces()`; severity/detail updates; new command reachability finding |
| `src/security/audit-trust-model.test.ts` | Control-plane and deny-path regression cases |
| `src/security/audit-plugins-trust.test.ts` | Native command surface mocks and command reachability cases |

## Non-goals and boundaries

- Does not change tool allow/deny enforcement at runtime.
- Does not add new config keys or env vars.
- Does not scan plugin command handlers for code safety (existing `--deep` plugin code scan remains separate).

target.title: fix(agents): retry transient filesystem races when reading workspace bootstrap files
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readWorkspaceFileWithGuards` in `src/agents/workspace.ts` reads each workspace
bootstrap file (AGENTS.md, SOUL.md, TOOLS.md, IDENTITY.md, USER.md, HEARTBEAT.md,
BOOTSTRAP.md, MEMORY.md) with a single `openRootFile` + `readFileSync(fd)` and no
retry. On a transient filesystem race (`EAGAIN`/`EWOULDBLOCK`/`EINTR` under load)
the read throws — or `openRootFile` returns `{ ok: false, reason: "io" }` — and the
file is reported `missing`. Because `loadWorkspaceBootstrapFiles` runs **every agent
turn** (`bootstrap-cache.ts`, "Refresh per turn so long-lived sessions pick up
edits"), a transient race silently drops the agent's bootstrap content for that
turn.

This is the unmigrated sibling of the transient-race fix in
`fileContentDiffersFromTemplate`: that function already retries reads via the
`retryAsync` + `isTransientWorkspaceReadError` helpers defined in this same file,
but the guard was only wired into the onboarding template check, not the per-turn
bootstrap reader.

## Why This Change Was Made

Wrap the reader's open+read in the existing in-file `retryAsync`
(`isTransientWorkspaceReadError`, 3 attempts, 50 ms) so a transient race is retried
instead of dropping the file. The retry re-opens on each attempt rather than
re-reading the same fd: retrying `readFileSync` on an already-partially-read fd
could return truncated content, whereas a fresh open gives a clean read and
`openRootFile`'s inode-identity guard still rejects a file swapped between attempts.
Transient failures on the open itself (surfaced by `openRootFile` as
`reason: "io"`) are retried too, so the fix is not one-sided within the function.

Behavior is otherwise unchanged: deterministic path/validation failures are not
retried, and exhausted transient retries still return `{ ok: false, reason: "io" }`
(surfaced as `missing`) rather than throwing — preserving this reader's existing
contract (unlike the template check, which propagates).

## User Impact

Long-lived agent sessions no longer intermittently lose their AGENTS/SOUL/TOOLS/
HEARTBEAT bootstrap content for a turn under filesystem load; the agent keeps its
identity and instructions across transient IO races.

## Evidence

- Three regression tests in `src/agents/workspace.test.ts` drive the real
  `loadWorkspaceBootstrapFiles` production path against a real temp workspace,
  injecting a transient `EAGAIN` at the `readFileSync`/`openSync` boundary:
  - a transient read on the first attempt is retried and the real content loads
    (not `missing`);
  - a transient open failure is retried and the content loads (not `missing`);
  - exhausted transient retries surface the file as `missing` without an uncaught
    throw.
- Focused suite `src/agents/workspace.test.ts` green — vitest reports `Tests 54
  passed (54)`, including the three new cases above.
- Core typecheck (`tsgo:core`, `tsgo:core:test`) clean; formatter and linter clean.

target.title: fix(runtime): throw typed ExitError instead of generic Error for simulated exit (#97796)
target.body:
Fixes #97796.

## What Problem This Solves

`createNonExitingRuntime().exit()` throws a generic `Error`, making it impossible for upstream `try-catch` handlers to distinguish a simulated process exit from a real runtime crash. Any code that needs to handle "exit requested but we're in a non-exiting runtime" differently from an actual error has no clean way to do so.

## Why This Change Was Made

Added an internal `ExitError` class (extending `Error`) that is thrown by `createNonExitingRuntime().exit()` instead of a generic `Error`. Callers can now use `instanceof ExitError` to distinguish simulated exits from real errors.

`ExitError` is intentionally kept **internal** — it is exported from `src/runtime.ts` for direct test imports, but is **not** re-exported from the public plugin SDK subpaths (`plugin-sdk/runtime.ts`, `plugin-sdk/runtime-env.ts`). This avoids expanding the public plugin SDK API surface without maintainer approval.

## User Impact

No user-facing impact. This is an internal runtime improvement for code that uses `createNonExitingRuntime`.

## Evidence

**Behavior addressed**: `createNonExitingRuntime().exit()` throws generic `Error` — no way to distinguish simulated exit from runtime crash.

**Real environment tested**: Node 24.13.1, local OpenClaw checkout.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:

```bash
node --import tsx -e "
import { createNonExitingRuntime, ExitError } from './src/runtime.js';
const rt = createNonExitingRuntime();
try { rt.exit(1); } catch (e) {
  console.log(JSON.stringify({
    isExitError: e instanceof ExitError,
    isError: e instanceof Error,
    name: e.name,
    code: e.code,
    message: e.message
  }));
}
"
```

**Evidence after fix**:

```
{"isExitError":true,"isError":true,"name":"ExitError","code":1,"message":"exit 1"}
```

Before fix: `e instanceof Error` is true but there's no way to know it's an exit vs a crash.
After fix: `e instanceof ExitError` cleanly distinguishes the two.

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/runtime.test.ts --run
```

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  8 passed (8)
```

- `exit function throws ExitError` — verifies typed error is thrown
- `ExitError includes exit code` — verifies code is preserved in message and instanceof
- `ExitError is distinguishable from generic Error` — NEW: proves instanceof ExitError works independently of instanceof Error

```bash
node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs src/runtime.ts src/runtime.test.ts
```

```
(passed, exit 0)
```

**Observed result after fix**: `createNonExitingRuntime().exit()` throws `ExitError` with the exit code and a descriptive message. Callers can use `instanceof ExitError` to distinguish simulated exits from real errors.

**What was not tested**: Upstream callers that currently catch the generic `Error` and would benefit from switching to `instanceof ExitError`. Those are follow-up work and not part of this change.

## Regression Test Plan

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/runtime.test.ts --run` — Test Files 1 passed (1), Tests 8 passed (8)
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs src/runtime.ts src/runtime.test.ts` — exit 0

## Root Cause

In `createNonExitingRuntime()`, the `exit` function throws `new Error(\`exit ${code}\`)` — a generic `Error` instance. Any upstream code that catches errors from the runtime cannot distinguish "the runtime simulated process.exit" from "something actually crashed." The fix adds a typed `ExitError` subclass so callers can use `instanceof` checks for clean control flow.

## AI Assistance

- **AI-assisted**: Yes
- **Model used**: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context)
- **Co-Authored-By**: Already in commit message

target.title: fix(gateway): stop accepting the Control UI token via ?token= query string
target.body:
## Summary

The Control UI assistant-media route (`/__openclaw__/assistant-media`) accepted the gateway shared secret — and paired operator device tokens — from a `?token=` URL query parameter (`allowQueryToken: true` in `src/gateway/control-ui.ts`). Secrets in URLs leak through reverse-proxy/CDN access logs, browser history, and the `Referer` header, and the gateway token is long-lived.

This contradicts the rest of the codebase:
- the hooks endpoint hard-rejects query tokens (`src/gateway/server/hooks-request-handler.ts`), and
- the Control UI itself warns that `?token=` "may appear in server logs" and prefers the URL fragment (`ui/src/ui/app-settings.ts`).

The legitimate browser flow doesn't need it: an authenticated `meta` request mints a signed, source-scoped, short-TTL `mediaTicket`, and the media fetch uses `?mediaTicket=`; programmatic clients send `Authorization: Bearer`. The first-party UI already uses `mediaTicket` exclusively.

### Change
- Delete `resolveAssistantMediaAuthToken` and `resolveControlUiReadAuthToken` and the `allowQueryToken` plumbing; Control UI read auth now resolves the token from `getBearerToken` only (header), or the signed `mediaTicket`. Net `control-ui.ts`: fewer paths.
- Existing media tests moved from `?token=` to `Authorization: Bearer`; the redundant query-auth device-token test removed (its header equivalent already exists).
- New e2e regression asserts a **correct** token in `?token=` is rejected while header + `mediaTicket` still serve media.

## Verification

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/control-ui.http.test.ts` → 220 passed
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/control-ui-assistant-media-query-token.e2e.test.ts` → 1 passed
- `oxfmt --check` + `oxlint` on changed files → clean; `pnpm tsgo:core` → 0 errors

### Real behavior proof
- Behavior addressed: the Control UI assistant-media route accepted the gateway shared secret (and paired operator device tokens) via the `?token=` URL query string, leaking a long-lived secret into reverse-proxy/CDN access logs, browser history, and the `Referer` header.
- Real environment tested: a real OpenClaw gateway HTTP server booted on loopback TCP via the gateway e2e harness (`withGatewayServer` → `startGatewayServer`); requests issued with real `fetch` against `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`. Node 22.22, Linux (WSL2).
- Exact steps or command run after this patch: drove one probe against a live gateway twice — first with the pre-fix file (`git show origin/main:src/gateway/control-ui.ts`), then with this PR's file — issuing `GET /__openclaw__/assistant-media` five ways via `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs`.
- Evidence after fix: live console output captured from the running gateway (`node` server, real loopback HTTP), before (pre-fix `origin/main`) vs after (this PR):
```text
BEFORE  origin/main src/gateway/control-ui.ts   (real gateway @ 127.0.0.1:62000)
  [1] no credential                    -> HTTP 401
  [2] ?token=<CORRECT gateway secret>  -> HTTP 200   secret-in-URL ACCEPTED  (the leak)
  [3] Authorization: Bearer <token>    -> HTTP 200
  [4] meta=1 (Bearer) -> mediaTicket   -> HTTP 200   available=true  ticket=v1.eyJzY29wZSI...
  [5] ?mediaTicket=<signed ticket>     -> HTTP 200

AFTER   this PR  src/gateway/control-ui.ts       (real gateway @ 127.0.0.1:33000)
  [1] no credential                    -> HTTP 401
  [2] ?token=<CORRECT gateway secret>  -> HTTP 401   secret-in-URL REJECTED  (the fix)
  [3] Authorization: Bearer <token>    -> HTTP 200   body="assistant media body"
  [4] meta=1 (Bearer) -> mediaTicket   -> HTTP 200   available=true  ticket=v1.eyJzY29wZSI...
  [5] ?mediaTicket=<signed ticket>     -> HTTP 200   body="assistant media body"
```
- Observed result after fix: only case [2] changed — a correct gateway secret in `?token=` went from HTTP 200 (accepted, pre-fix) to HTTP 401 (rejected). The legitimate `Authorization: Bearer` header and the signed `mediaTicket` browser path still serve media unchanged. The PR's e2e regression fails on pre-fix code and passes on the fix.
- What was not tested: full `pnpm check` / CI matrix (left to CI); no UI/browser change (the first-party UI already uses `mediaTicket`).

target.title: fix(agents): route provider-local-service health probe through fetchWithSsrFGuard
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The `probeHealth` function in `src/agents/provider-local-service.ts:260` polls the operator-configured `service.healthUrl` via the un-guarded global `fetch`. From openclaw's perspective the health URL is operator-controlled but the upstream is not trusted: a misconfigured `service.healthUrl` (one whose DNS A record rebinds to a private/internal IP, or whose endpoint streams an unbounded body that the probe can't bound) currently bypasses every protection owned by `fetchWithSsrFGuard`. `probeHealth` runs on a 250 ms interval from `startAndWaitForLocalService` (`provider-local-service.ts:301`) until the local service becomes healthy, so an SSRF miss here is amplified into a repeated fetch loop against the hostile target.

This PR wraps the probe fetch with `fetchWithSsrFGuard` in STRICT mode and feeds it a narrow local-service SSRF policy (`resolveLocalServiceProbePolicy`) that supports loopback literal URLs (`127.0.0.1`, `::1`, `localhost`) without making public hostnames bypass the private-network block. The existing `.catch(...).finally(...)` chain (timeout translation, `controller.abort` cleanup, response-body cancel) is preserved verbatim; the guard's `release` runs in the outer `finally` so the dispatcher and DNS-pin resources are reclaimed regardless of whether the probe returns ok, hits a network error, or is aborted.

## Changes

- `src/agents/provider-local-service.ts:5,13-14` — add `import { isLoopbackIpAddress } from "@openclaw/net-policy/ip"` and `import type { SsrFPolicy } from "../infra/net/ssrf.js"`.
- `src/agents/provider-local-service.ts:222-263` — add `resolveLocalServiceProbePolicy(url)` helper. For loopback literal hostnames (`127.0.0.1`, `::1` unwrapped, `localhost`) it returns `{ allowedHostnames: [literal], hostnameAllowlist: [literal] }` so the guard skips private-network checks for the literal loopback. For any other hostname it returns `{ hostnameAllowlist: [hostname] }` only — the hostname check passes, but the guard still validates resolved IPs against the private-network block, so a public-looking healthUrl that DNS-resolves to a private IP is rejected. This addresses the round-1 ClawSweeper finding that target-derived `allowedHostnames` made every configured hostname bypass the private-network block (`ssrf.ts:229` `shouldSkipPrivateNetworkChecks`).
- `src/agents/provider-local-service.ts:274-279` — `probeHealth` now calls `policy: resolveLocalServiceProbePolicy(url)` instead of the prior target-derived `policy: { allowedHostnames: [new URL(url).hostname] }`. The existing `clearTimeout`, `removeEventListener("abort", onAbort)`, and `await response?.body?.cancel?.()` cleanup runs unchanged.
- `src/agents/provider-local-service.test.ts` — 5 new policy unit tests (loopback IPv4, loopback IPv6, `localhost`, public hostname, look-local-but-isn't hostname) and 1 new end-to-end negative control (`blocks health probe when public-looking healthUrl resolves to a private IP via DNS rebind`) that injects a `lookupFn` returning `192.168.1.1` for a public-looking URL and asserts the guard rejects with `resolves to private`. The existing 12 tests drive `ensureModelProviderLocalService` end-to-end against real loopback and continue to pass unchanged.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed**: `probeHealth` now routes its GET to `service.healthUrl` through `fetchWithSsrFGuard` with a narrow local-service policy; DNS rebinding protection and the private-network block now apply to public-looking healthUrl hostnames while explicit loopback probe URLs still resolve and reach the local service.
- **Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64, Node 22.19, `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/provider-local-service.test.ts --run`
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
  ```bash
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/provider-local-service.test.ts --run
  ```
- **Evidence after fix**:
  ```
  Test Files  1 passed (1)
       Tests  18 passed (18)
    Start at  23:46:01
    Duration  4.36s
  ```
  - 12 pre-existing tests pass unchanged (real loopback probes via `freePort()` + `process.execPath` + inline `http.createServer` flow through the guard and succeed).
  - 5 new policy unit tests pass:
    - IPv4 loopback literal `http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1/models` → `{ allowedHostnames: ["127.0.0.1"], hostnameAllowlist: ["127.0.0.1"] }` (loopback literal accepted, private check skipped for the literal).
    - IPv6 loopback literal `http://[::1]:11434/v1/models` → `{ allowedHostnames: ["::1"], hostnameAllowlist: ["::1"] }` (URL brackets stripped before loopback check + allowlist).
    - `http://localhost:11434/v1/models` → `{ allowedHostnames: ["localhost"], hostnameAllowlist: ["localhost"] }` (operator-friendly alias works).
    - `http://api.example.com/v1/models` → `{ hostnameAllowlist: ["api.example.com"] }` only — `allowedHostnames` is **absent** (private-network block preserved against DNS rebind).
    - `http://my-service.internal/v1/models` → `hostnameAllowlist: ["my-service.internal"]` only — the `.internal` suffix does not bypass private checks.
  - 1 new end-to-end negative control test (`blocks health probe when public-looking healthUrl resolves to a private IP via DNS rebind`) passes: it calls `fetchWithSsrFGuard` directly with `resolveLocalServiceProbePolicy("http://api.example.com/v1/models")` and a `lookupFn` returning `192.168.1.1`. The guard rejects with `Blocked: resolves to private/internal/special-use IP address` and `fetchImpl` is never invoked. Reverting the helper back to the target-derived `allowedHostnames: [new URL(url).hostname]` shape makes this test fail (the private-network block is skipped for `api.example.com`).
- **Observed result after fix**: Real loopback probes continue to flow end-to-end through the guard, and a real public-looking URL with a hostile DNS-rebind answer is rejected before any network I/O. The narrow policy shape is the inverse of the round-1 finding: the only hostnames that get `allowedHostnames` (which triggers the private-network-check skip) are the loopback literals `127.0.0.1`, `::1`, and `localhost`.
- **What was not tested**: Live probe against a real managed local service deployment; the proof is unit-level via the production wrapper + loopback for the happy path and via the guard's own DNS-rebind path for the negative control, the same shape approved for prior fetch-guard wiring PRs.

## Out of scope (separate follow-ups)

- `src/agents/runtime/proxy.ts:299` (`streamProxy`) — sibling surface with the same pattern, submitted as a separate PR to keep each change XS.
- `src/agents/minimax-vlm.ts` and `src/infra/push-apns.relay.ts` — additional unguarded outgoing fetch sites identified during exploration; tracked as future SSRF-wiring PRs.

## Risk

- **Scope**: 1 prod file + 1 test file; +45 source LoC (net) + 61 test LoC.
- **Behavior**: Same outgoing request shape as before, plus a narrow policy object routed through `resolveLocalServiceProbePolicy`. `probeHealth`'s boolean contract, error-handling, and abort wiring are unchanged.
- **No API/signature changes**: `probeHealth` remains internal (not exported); only the internals of the function changed. `resolveLocalServiceProbePolicy` is a new export added to this module specifically so the test can verify the policy shape directly.
- **Compatibility**: All 12 pre-existing tests pass unchanged. The probe response-body `cancel()` in the outer `finally` still runs after `releaseGuarded()` so backpressure cleanup is preserved.
- **Type check**: `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs` clean on the touched branch.
- **Lint**: `node scripts/run-oxlint-shards.mjs --threads=4` clean (all three shards).
- **Sibling coordination**: Distinct file from `proxy.ts`; submitted as a separate PR. The new helper reuses the canonical `isLoopbackIpAddress` from `@openclaw/net-policy/ip` (same package `configured-local-origin-bypass.ts:3` imports for the analogous check).

target.title: refactor(qa): add canonical live channel adapters
target.body:
Closes #99699

## What Problem This Solves

Telegram, Slack, WhatsApp, and Matrix live QA transports could not be selected by the shared QA Lab scenario host. Matrix also belongs to its own QA runner plugin, so QA Lab needs an owner-neutral contribution contract rather than importing plugin-private runtime code.

## Why This Change Was Made

Each live channel contributes a transport adapter definition through the existing QA runner registration seam. QA Lab remains the single scenario host: it owns the QA bus, wait lifecycle, failure detection, and state-backed adapter wrapper, while channel factories own only transport setup, inbound delivery, outbound observation, readiness, cleanup, and channel configuration.

The runner contract now exposes only four adapter setup options and a three-method message recorder instead of duplicating the full CLI option object and QA bus state. Telegram Bot API types come from the Telegram plugin API, and Slack message types are derived from the existing validated response schema.

The existing `qa telegram`, `qa slack`, `qa whatsapp`, and `qa matrix` commands keep their current runners and scenario catalogs. The shared host can run migrated scenarios with `qa suite --channel-driver live --channel <adapter-id>` without changing current command behavior. Matrix cleanup and forced-exit behavior remain intact.

QA Channel and Crabline keep their existing stateful implementations; contributed live definitions are the only transports wrapped by the shared host. Slack streamed previews are reconciled into QA bus edit events when the native message is updated in place.

## User Impact

Existing live QA commands behave as before. Maintainers can migrate shared YAML/flow scenarios to the canonical adapters incrementally, then remove legacy scenario runners only after their command contracts are represented by the shared host.

Explicit shared live-adapter runs use one worker, reject runtime-pair duplication, and default to the selected factory's declared canonical scenarios.

## Evidence

- Rebased onto `bfffa950d71c91b5a8f9c2f3bbd2d3a80da7705c`.
- Focused SDK, QA host, registry, Crabline, CLI, Telegram, Slack, and boundary tests passed.

target.title: feat(context-engine): add reference context channel
target.body:
Closes #88753

## What Problem This Solves

Context-engine authors need a safe way to provide historical summaries, memories, or retrieved context without encoding that data as fresh current-user input or higher-authority prompt additions. Without a dedicated lane, compacted/reference data can regain too much prompt authority or interfere with provider message constraints.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds a narrow `AssembleResult.referenceContext` SDK lane plus a `reference-context` host capability. Native Codex app-server hosts now project that lane into Codex `turn/start.additionalContext` with `kind: "untrusted"`, so Codex owns the lower-authority external-fragment rendering instead of OpenClaw splicing the data into `turn/start.input`.

Embedded OpenClaw runs no longer advertise `reference-context`; they still support `assemble-before-prompt`, but engines that require a true reference-context lane are rejected there until embedded has an equivalent non-message transport.

## User Impact

Context-engine and plugin developers can return historical/reference data separately from executable model-history messages. Users get safer continuity because native Codex receives the reference data through its dedicated additional-context protocol lane while chat-only/current-user prompt text stays focused on the current request.

## Evidence

Real behavior proof from a redacted local OpenClaw `runCodexAppServerAttempt` test using a fake app-server client that captures the outgoing `turn/start` params:

```text
turn/start.input contains current request: true
turn/start.input contains OpenClaw reference context: false
turn/start.additionalContext.openclaw_reference_context.kind: untrusted
turn/start.additionalContext.openclaw_reference_context.value contains reference summary: true
```

Real Codex app-server proof using installed `@openai/codex` 0.142.4, `codex app-server --listen stdio://`, isolated `CODEX_HOME`, and a local mock `/v1/responses` server:

```text
responseRequestCount: 1
model request contains current prompt "inspect tab": true
model request contains external reference fragment: true
external fragment:
<external_openclaw_reference_context>OpenClaw reference context for this turn:
- Reference note: browser tab title is Example Domain.</external_openclaw_reference_context>

model input item summary:
- developer instructions item
- AGENTS/environment context item
- separate user item with <external_openclaw_reference_context>...</external_openclaw_reference_context>
- separate current user item: inspect tab
```

Additional real Codex app-server clear/replace proof with the same installed app-server and mock `/v1/responses` server:

```text
turn 1 additionalContext value: Reference A
turn 1 user text order: ... external Reference A, first turn

turn 2 additionalContext value: Reference B
turn 2 user text order: ... external Reference A, first turn, external Reference B, second turn

turn 3 additionalContext omitted
turn 3 user text order: ... external Reference A, first turn, external Reference B, second turn, third turn no reference
thirdTurnHasNewExternalImmediatelyBeforePrompt: false
```

That matches Codex core behavior: `AdditionalContextStore::merge(values)` replaces the retained map with the current turn's map, and omitted app-server `additionalContext` maps to an empty map. Prior external fragments remain only as ordinary earlier transcript history; no fresh `openclaw_reference_context` fragment is injected before the current prompt when OpenClaw omits reference context.

Codex source contract checked locally in sibling `../codex`:

- `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/turn.rs` defines experimental `turn/start.additionalContext` as camelCase `additionalContext`.
- `codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/turn_processor.rs` maps omitted `additionalContext` to an empty core map.
- `codex-rs/core/src/state/additional_context.rs` replaces the retained additional-context map on each turn.
- `codex-rs/context-fragments/src/additional_context.rs` renders untrusted entries as `<external_{key}>...</external_{key}>` fragments.
- `codex-rs/app-server/tests/suite/v2/turn_start.rs` covers `turn_start_additional_context_flows_to_model_input`.
- `codex-rs/core/tests/suite/additional_context.rs` covers replacement/removal behavior and additional context being model-visible without becoming the current user turn item.

target.title: fix(codex): resolve dynamic tool hard timeout from timeoutSeconds when timeoutMs is absent
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a dynamic tool call passes `timeoutSeconds` (e.g. `{ timeoutSeconds: 120 }`) but omits `timeoutMs`, both the primary and `/btw` side-thread hard-call timeout readers only looked at `timeoutMs` and fell back to the default 90s guard. Tools that explicitly set a longer timeout in seconds (e.g. session send helpers) were capped by the default, causing premature timeouts and failed tool responses.

Fixes [#98864](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/98864).

## Why This Change Was Made

Both the primary (`dynamic-tool-execution.ts`) and side-thread (`side-question.ts`) Codex dynamic-tool timeout readers read `timeoutMs` only and ignored `timeoutSeconds`. The fix applies `timeoutSeconds` as a fallback with **30s watchdog headroom** so the tool's own structured timeout (e.g. `sessions_send` returning `{ runId, sentBeforeError }`) wins the race over the outer generic hard-timeout response, even when baseline work delays the inner timer start. Fractional `timeoutSeconds` values are rejected via `Number.isInteger` to match `sessions_send` integer validation.

### Behavior rules

| Priority | Input | Outcome |
|----------|-------|---------|
| 1 | `timeoutMs` is valid positive number | Use `timeoutMs` (no headroom, existing behavior) |
| 2 | `timeoutMs` absent/invalid, `timeoutSeconds` valid integer | Use `timeoutSeconds * 1000 + 30s headroom` (**new**) |
| 3 | `timeoutSeconds` is fractional or invalid | Ignored (matches `sessions_send` integer contract) |
| 4 | Both absent/invalid | Fall back to configured or default timeout (existing) |

## User Impact

- **Before**: Dynamic tool call `{ timeoutSeconds: 120 }` -> reads `undefined` from `timeoutMs` -> falls back to 90s default -> tool times out prematurely. Affected both primary and `/btw` side-thread calls.
- **After**: Dynamic tool call `{ timeoutSeconds: 120 }` -> reads `150000` (120s + 30s headroom) -> watchdog gives the tool enough time to return its own structured result -> `sessions_send` structured `{ runId, sentBeforeError }` reaches caller before watchdog fires.

`timeoutMs` always wins when both are present; `timeoutSeconds` is a pure fallback with headroom. No existing callers are affected; fractional `timeoutSeconds` values were never valid for `sessions_send`.

## Evidence

### Unit Tests (60/60 passed)

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-execution.test.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/side-question.test.ts
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  60 passed (60)
```

Primary path: +4 tests (fallback w/ 30s headroom, timeoutMs precedence, fractional rejection, invalid value)
Side-thread path: +3 tests (fallback w/ 30s headroom, timeoutMs precedence, fractional rejection)

### Real Machine Runtime Verification

**Environment**: Linux x64, Node v24.18.0

```
Primary: timeoutSeconds=120     -> 150000 ✅
Primary: timeoutMs=30000+ts=120 -> 30000  ✅
Primary: timeoutSeconds=120.5   -> 90000  ✅ (fractional rejected)
Primary: no timeout fields      -> 90000  ✅ (default)

Side:    timeoutSeconds=120     -> 150000 ✅
Side:    timeoutMs=30000+ts=120 -> 30000  ✅
```

### Verification Summary

| Scenario | Primary | Side-thread |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `timeoutSeconds=120`, no `timeoutMs` | ✅ 150000 | ✅ 150000 |
| `timeoutMs=30000` + `timeoutSeconds=120` | ✅ 30000 (wins) | ✅ 30000 (wins) |
| Fractional `timeoutSeconds=120.5` | ✅ Default | ✅ Default |
| Neither field | ✅ Default | ✅ Default |

## Changes

| File | Changed | Notes |
|------|---------|-------|
| `dynamic-tool-execution.ts` | +30s headroom, timeoutSeconds fallback, integer-only guard | `readDynamicToolCallTimeoutMs` + `readTimeoutSecondsAsMs` |
| `side-question.ts` | Same pattern for `/btw` path | `readSideDynamicToolCallTimeoutMs` + `readSideTimeoutSecondsAsMs` |
| `dynamic-tool-execution.test.ts` | +4 tests | fallback, precedence, fractional, invalid |
| `side-question.test.ts` | +3 tests | fallback, precedence, fractional |

target.title: fix(feishu): avoid mention forwarding when bot open id is unavailable
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Feishu direct-message mention forwarding could be triggered when the bot open id was unavailable. In that state, ordinary user mentions were treated as mention-forward targets even though OpenClaw could not reliably know whether the bot was addressed.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Feishu mention-forward check now stops early when the bot open id is missing, so it only evaluates “bot plus other user” or direct-message mention forwarding when the bot identity is known. This keeps the change scoped to mention-forward detection and does not change Feishu message parsing, broadcast mention filtering, or outbound mention formatting.

## User Impact

Feishu users should no longer see accidental mention-forward behavior during bot identity probe/configuration gaps. Normal mention forwarding remains unchanged when the bot open id is available.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(gateway): redact Responses media blocks in chat history sanitization
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users viewing chat history in Control UI / WebChat would still receive embedded `data:` image payloads on Responses-style media blocks (`input_image.image_url` and legacy `image.url`) after history sanitization, even though other base64 and data-URL media paths were already redacted.

Also fixes CI failures in `chat.directive-tags.test.ts`: live WebChat broadcast must keep `{ type: "input_image", image_url: "data:..." }` for QR/image delivery, so inline media redaction is scoped to history-only paths.

ClawSweeper follow-up: mixed-case data URLs such as `DATA:image/png;BASE64,...` could bypass history redaction because sanitization used case-sensitive `startsWith("data:")`.

## Why This Change Was Made

`sanitizeChatHistoryContentBlock()` now treats Responses media blocks the same as existing image/audio redaction when `redactInlineMedia: true` is passed from history paths only. Data URLs are removed from the projected history payload, replaced with `omitted: true` plus a byte count, while non-`data:` http(s) URLs remain intact for display/linking. Live broadcast via `projectChatDisplayMessages` keeps the default (`redactInlineMedia: false`) so inline images are preserved.

Data URL detection for history redaction reuses `classifyMediaReferenceSource().isDataUrl` (`/^data:/i`) via a local `isInlineDataUrl()` helper, matching `src/media/media-reference.ts` and closing the mixed-case bypass.

All chat.history-style callers now opt in: main gateway (`chat.ts`), session SSE snapshots (`session-history-state.ts`), embedded gateway stub, and TUI embedded backend.

## User Impact

Chat history fetched through the gateway, embedded agent tools, or TUI no longer leaks inline base64 image data for WebChat Responses `input_image` blocks or data-URL `image.url` blocks. Operators and users still see that media was present (via `omitted` + `bytes`) without shipping the raw payload over the wire. Remote https image links continue to display normally. Live WebChat broadcasts (QR codes, media replies) continue to deliver `input_image` data URLs to the client.

## Evidence

### Unit tests

- sanitizer shapes: `input_image.image_url`, `image.url`, `image.source.data`, nested `image_url.url`, mixed-case `DATA:...`, https preservation, broadcast preservation

- TUI embedded backend: `loadHistory` passes `redactInlineMedia: true` to `projectRecentChatDisplayMessages`

### Real WS gateway endpoint proof (live Gateway + on-disk transcript)
